# Rapid Access to 3-Substituted Bicyclo[1.1.1]pentanes

**Authors:** Katherine I. Burton; David W. C. MacMillan

**Affiliations:** 1Merck Center for Catalysis at Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States | 2Lead contact

## Abstract

The prevalence of benzene rings in pharmaceutical scaffolds has prompted efforts to identify structural bioisosteres with improved in vivo properties. Notably, bicyclo[1.1.1]pentanes (BCPs)—C(sp3)-enriched, 1,4-disubstituted phenyl bioisosteres—have been leveraged to tune the pharmacokinetic profiles of lead compounds. While 3-arylated BCPs have been widely implemented to confer resistance against oxidative degradation and hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) processes, the analogous 3-alkylated BCPs remain underexplored as bioisosteric “benzylic” C–H motifs. Current methods to install 3-alkylated BCP motifs are heavily reliant on lengthy de novo synthesis and the preparation of reactive [1.1.1]propellane feedstocks, limiting their adoption in drug discovery programs. In this report, we disclose a mild, unified method for the preparation of both alkyl and aryl-substituted BCPs from bench-stable precursors. This method, which proceeds via dual copper-photoredox catalysis, is capable of installing BCP functionalities onto a range of saturated motifs, aryl-containing residues, and medicinally relevant heterocycles.

## Abstract

Growing interest in C(sp3)-rich bioisosteres has driven efforts to synthetically manipulate bicyclo[1.1.1]pentane (BCP) scaffolds. The strained geometry of BCPs imparts high C(sp3)-H bond dissociation energies that enhance the metabolic stability of the carbocycle. However, quaternary, 3-alkylated BCPs remain underdeveloped as bioisosteres of benzylic environments. The reported method enables access to 3-alkylated and 3-arylated BCPs under mild photoredox conditions using commercially abundant precursors.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

The selective tuning of absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion-toxicity (ADMET) properties is a critical component of drug design. Notably, incorporation of a higher fraction of sp3-hybridized atoms (Fsp3) leads to improved solubility,1 reduced off-target binding promiscuity, and enhanced likelihood of clinical success.2,3 The strategic installation of Fsp3-rich bioisosteres can permit selective modulation of pharmacokinetic profiles while retaining physiological efficacy.4–6 Arenes are prevalent in pharmaceuticals, yet oxidative degradation pathways can lead to in vivo toxicity while promoting rapid metabolic excretion.7 To tune the therapeutic index of a lead candidate, judicious evaluation of both bioavailability and drug stability is critical.8 Accordingly, the selective incorporation of 3-substituted BCPs as 1,4-disubstituted phenyl ring bioisosteres has been shown to improve the thermodynamic solubility of parent molecules while suppressing oxidative metabolism.9,10 Owing to their rigid geometry and consequently inert aliphatic C–H bonds, 3-substituted BCPs recapitulate the geometric exit vectors exhibited in para-substituted aryl rings (Scheme 1, top).11 We proposed that quaternized 3-alkylated BCPs could offer synthetic access to stabilized bioisosteric pseudo “benzylic” environments that would otherwise present metabolic weak points in a traditional aryl scaffold (see supplemental information, Section S2 and Table S1, Section S3). A number of elegant C(sp2) installation strategies have been disclosed, including carbene insertion,12 atom transfer radical addition (ATRA),13,14 and strain-release paradigms.15–19 However, incorporation of tertiary C(sp3)-functionalization remains synthetically challenging and heavily reliant on preparation of [1.1.1]propellane or pre-activation strategies.20–22 Further, established methods can suffer functional group compatibility issues, arising from the need for harsh conditions and reactive precursors. Consequently, late-stage BCP incorporation frequently requires de novo synthesis and multistep re-routes, ultimately severely impacting the total number of industrial patents encompassing alkylated BCP motifs (Figure 1, middle).23,24

We aimed to address this outstanding challenge by developing a mild coupling platform, capable of delivering a diverse array of both 3-alkylated or 3-arylated BCPs in a single-step, one-flask protocol. To this end, we were inspired by N-hydroxyphthalimide redox-active ester-functionalized BCPs as attractive, bench-stable alternatives to reactive propellane feedstocks (Scheme 1, bottom).25–29 The reported transformation seeks to expand on prior methods by introducing a modular platform capable of selective site functionalization, which should prove useful for late-stage installation of drug motifs, without reliance on stoichiometric zinc or Hantzsch ester reductants, organolithium, Grignard, or reactive strain-release reagents.30–33 We report an expansion of accessible chemical space via rapid access to alkyl bromides; a challenge underexplored by. The reported method is designed to satisfy three key goals: (1). Obviate reliance on stoichiometric metal reagents. Prior art relies extensively on organometallics as coupling partners and stochiometric metals (e.g. Zn) as reductants. This current method uses neither, in the interest of improving functional group compatibility and accessing more diverse chemical space. (2). Circumvent reliance on [1.1.1]propellane for 3–functionalization. The necessary calibration of [1.1.1.]propellane stock solutions to monitor precursor decomposition offers potential for improvement in any coupling regime. (3). Deliver access to greater chemical space alongside improved synthetic modularity. This method does not rely on strain-release to achieve 3-functionalization and therefore seeks to enable sequential or late-stage functionalization.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

### Reaction development

At the outset, we focused on developing a BCP 3-functionalization method centered on a platform of convenience and modularity. Traditional methods require that [1.1.1]propellane be prepared from organolithium reagents and distilled immediately prior to use. By contrast, we envisioned employing one universal, bench-stable building block amenable to diverse functionalization. Specifically, the activated BCP acid (Scheme 2, structure 9) was viewed as a convenient precursor for radical generation.

Transition metal-catalyzed alkyl-alkyl cross-couplings have traditionally been beset by multiple challenges, including competitive β-hydride elimination and sluggish elementary activation steps.34 Circumventing strain-release or multi-step paradigms to access 3-alkylation was a particular consideration, as traditional nickel-mediated routes offer restrictive access to aromatic, or sp2 coupling partners. To bypass these obstacles, we envisioned harnessing copper as a broadly tolerant catalytic platform able to undergo kinetically facile reductive elimination predisposed towards C(sp2) and C(sp3)-BCP bond formation. Copper-mediated cross-coupling reactions traditionally rely on air- and moisture-sensitive transmetalation reagents to overcome a kinetically challenging oxidative addition step.35,36 To avoid using these sensitive organolithium/Grignard reagents, which can present challenges in late-stage settings, we proposed to employ a mild photocatalytic platform to unveil the radical coupling partners from abundant halide precursors. We chose to utilize readily available alkyl bromides instead of the more expensive, reductively labile alkyl iodide precursors.1 To this end, our laboratory previously disclosed the use of open-shell silicon reagents to selectively activate organohalides via a polarity-matched halogen atom transfer (XAT) event.37,38 This XAT event would be expected to proceed on orders greater than k~106 M−1s−1 to provide the key alkyl radical species.39–41 Crucially, by using an aminosilane reagent we simultaneously sidestep reliance on harsh (e.g. Zn) reductants, while achieving mild access to the desired XAT event. Next, a reductive pathway would achieve photocatalyst (PC) turnover and concurrently unveil the BCP bridgehead radical, capable of capture by the copper catalyst.42

The proposed reaction mechanism is outlined in Scheme 2. PC 1 [2,4,5,6-tetrakis(9H-carbazol-9-yl)isophthalonitrile (4CzIPN)] accesses a long-lived, triplet excited state under blue light irradiation (τ=5.1s, E1/2 = +1.35 V vs saturated calomel electrode (SCE) in MeCN).38 The excited state, 2, is reduced by aminosilane reagent 4 to generate 3, which undergoes single electron reduction (SET) of N-hydroxyphthalimide (NHPI)-functionalized BCP ester, 9, to promote decarboxylative formation of radical 10 while regenerating PC 1 and an equivalent of phthalimide anion. Activation of CuBr2 (11a) is feasible under this photocatalyst regime (E1/2 [4CzIPN/4CzIPN−•= −1.21 V vs SCE]) to afford Cu(I) species (11b). Intermediate 10 is postulated to undergo radical trapping into copper catalyst 11b to afford Cu(II)–BCP intermediate 12. Simultaneously, oxidative activation of aminosilane reagent 4 is hypothesized to furnish radical cation 5, which undergoes base-mediated substitution at silicon and α-trimethylsilyl group migration to unveil nucleophilic silyl radical 6.43 A polarity-matched XAT event with unactivated alkyl bromide 7 liberates one equivalent of carbon-centered radical 8. Subsequent radical trapping is postulated to occur at near diffusion-controlled rates (k~109 M−1s−1) to furnish Cu(III) intermediate 13.44 A favorable inner sphere reductive elimination is proposed to promote bond formation, regenerating catalytically active Cu(I) while delivering the target 3-substituted BCP product.

Extensive optimization studies revealed that combining alkyl bromide with tert-butyl-methyl-aminosilane reagent 4 (2.0 equiv), NHPI-BCP 9 (1.5 equiv), CuBr2 (20 mol%), sodium acetate (2.0 equiv), and 4CzIPN (1 mol%), followed by subsequent irradiation in the presence of acetone [0.05M] furnished the desired product in optimal yield (SI, Table S2). Further studies revealed that higher photocatalyst loadings (10 mol% 4CzIPN) could be used to furnish the product 36 in 78% yield (see Supplementary Information). As expected, no product was observed in the absence of silane, photocatalyst, or light (see SI, Figure S18 for control studies). We hypothesize that successful execution of the proposed transformation requires careful control of the relative rates of the XAT and decarboxylation steps. We recognize that tuning the relative rates of radical generation is critical for achieving efficient Cu speciation and therein attaining a kinetically favorable reductive elimination while minimizing unproductive pathways.45 Accordingly, suppression of competing protodehalogenation and homodimerization byproducts was ultimately achieved via attenuation of silane equivalencies and copper catalyst loading.

With optimal conditions in hand, we sought to examine the alkylation scope for this transformation (Figure 1). We were delighted to find that a variety of unactivated primary bromides were well-tolerated (14–23, 46–57% yield). The mild reaction conditions enabled extension of this platform to drug core moieties,46 furnishing a BCP-functionalized isoxazole derivative (14, 46% yield) and protected aminopyrimidine (15, 56% yield) in synthetically useful yields. Further, the protocol enables direct access to β-amino pharmaceutical derivatives, as exemplified by the phenethylamine bioisostere (16, 56% yield). We also observed rapid incorporation of the BCP scaffold into medicinally relevant heterocycles to generate oxadiazole (17, 57% yield). This protocol further permits incorporation of the BCP bioisostere into the 2-benzoxazolone core of FDA-approved pharmaceutical Chlorzoxazone (18, 50% yield). The incorporation of synthetically relevant linchpins for post-derivatization was demonstrated via a primary amine surrogate (19, 53% yield) and pendant pyridyl chloride (20, 50% yield). Given the diverse pharmaceutical profile of triazoles and their use in antifungal agents,47 we were pleased to demonstrate the compatibility of this net redox-neutral method with a triazole functionality (21, 57% yield). As an extension of this platform, we next evaluated C–C bond formation between the BCP carbocycle (strain energy~65–68 kcal mol-1)48 and strained coupling partners. We were delighted to note translatability between secondary acyclic (24, 72% yield), and cyclic (25, 63% yield) environments. We further demonstrated the compatibility of a diverse range of electronically and topologically differentiated secondary bromide substrates (24–41, 30–72% yield). A collective desire to increase F(sp3) character has prompted growing interest in spirocyclic scaffolds, the 3-dimensionality of which helps to suppress off-target binding promiscuity in late-stage drug candidates.49 We sought to investigate the compatibility of alkyl spirocyclic coupling partners in our method. We generated a library of previously undocumented BCP-coupled carbocyclic motifs, including select permutations of 4,6- (27, 40% yield), 4,4- (29, 30% yield), 6,6- (30, 54% yield), 5,4- (31, 59% yield), and 5,6- (33, 70% yield) spirocycles. These efforts yielded a diverse range of BCP structural motifs bearing three and four quaternary centers. Moreover, we successfully synthesized scaffold 32 (58% yield) to access a tetracyclic BCP motif.

Recognizing the prevalence of piperidine motifs across diverse pharmaceutical classes,50 we were gratified to observe the streamlined incorporation of BCP bioisosteres into these scaffolds (36, 63% yield; 37, 54% yield). To explore the limits of functional group compatibility, we further tested this methodology on substrates bearing stereochemical information. Thus, the nitrogen-functionalized compound, 28, was accessed in 50% yield, while further exploration of chemical space furnished the tetrahydropyran scaffold 39 in 54% yield (2.33:1 d.r.). We next pursued α-bromo amides (34, 50% yield, 38, 49% yield) to demonstrate the compatibility of electron-deficient radicals with this method. Finally, the platform was amenable to tertiary bromide substrates, furnishing contiguous quaternary centers in synthetically useful yield (42, 31% yield).

Despite their prevalence in approved small-molecule drugs, phenols are susceptible to rapid excretion due to their hydroxylated cores.51 Difluoromethyl functionalities have been harnessed as bioisosteres of alcohol groups, in part due to their advantageous retention of hydrogen-bonding activity.52 Consequently, we sought to access phenol bioisosteres by extending our BCP protocol to difluoromethylation. We were pleased to find that the desired adduct, 41, could be accessed in 42% assay yield in a single step from simple starting materials.

### Extension of reaction design to incorporate (hetero)aryl halides

Flat, sp2-rich environments are pervasive in drug discovery,2,53 historically arising from the prevalence of robust synthetic strategies, such as Suzuki-Miyaura couplings, that facilitate rapid C(sp2) fragment installation.54 By contrast, the synthetic challenges associated with incorporating 3-dimensionality into drug scaffolds have limited expansion in this area. Consequently, we sought to devise a single platform capable of accessing both alkylated and arylated BCPs to furnish bioisosteres of biaryl environments. We envisioned that a broadly tolerant, modular platform towards BCP motif construction would potentially accelerate the design of new drug analogs.

To this end, we were pleased to find that BCPs could be appended to an array of electronically diverse aryl and heteroaryl bromides under modified conditions (Figure 2, 43–59, 40–66% yields). Notably, these conditions enabled facile 3-arylation without the need for organogrignards, [1.1.1]propellane, or forcing conditions (see SI for further details).27 Given the value of fluorine motifs in drug discovery,55 we were delighted to observe trifluoromethyl groups were tolerated in the reaction conditions (43, 52% yield). Further, we successfully incorporated cross-coupling partners for post-functionalization (44, 50% yield), opening avenues to downstream diversification. In line with this logic, nitrile-substituted scaffolds (45, 57% yield, 46, 52% yield, and 48, 50% yield) offer synthetic handles for downstream redox manipulations. In investigating the effects of strain in drug-relevant architectures, we observed cyclopropyl group incorporation can correlate with improved drug candidate progression from preclinical to clinical phase trials.56 Accordingly, we were gratified to find cyclopropane exit vectors were tolerated under the reported method (46 and 47, 52% and 41% yield, respectively). A series of medicinally relevant heterocycles was next investigated (49–59, 40–66% yields), with a particular focus on pharmaceutically privileged nitrogen-containing structures. Varied aryl substitution patterns were accessed, including electron-deficient pyridyl motifs (49–56, 40–66% yield); quinoxaline scaffolds (57, 43% yield), phthalide (58, 42% yield), and pyrazolo-pyridines (59, 49% yield; see SI for additional examples, and SI Section 7, Figure S26 S32 to demonstrate an example inspired from an industrial patent).

### Incorporation of drug-relevant motifs

Finally, we examined the applicability of the method toward the incorporation of drug-like motifs (Figure 3). Encouraged by an operationally facile functionalization of the quinolinone core of the anti-psychotic Aripiprazole (60, 64% yield), we next accessed a Tafamidis analogue (61, 50% yield). Direct functionalization of the commercially available anti-fungal bromuconazole was achieved in synthetically useful yield (62, 32% yield), alongside the synthesis of BCP functionalized 6-chloropyridazine (63, 51% yield). These results collectively demonstrate tolerance of our operationally streamlined approach to a variety of complex, densely functionalized heterocycles bearing aryl halides and alternate synthetic handles. To probe the translatability of this method to alternate bioisosteric environments, modified arylation conditions were demonstrated using an oxa-bicyclo[2.1.1]hexane redox-active ester fragment to attain product in 42% yield versus 1,4-difluorobenzene (see SI, example Figure S27 for details).

## Conclusion

In conclusion, we have demonstrated the rapid incorporation of 3-substituted BCPs into diverse alkyl and (hetero)aryl coupling partners via the implementation of a bench-stable BCP precursor under mild metallaphotoredox conditions. This coupling protocol is operationally robust and broadly tolerant to a variety of substrate electronics. We have shown that the mild conditions of the reported procedure allow broad functional group compatibility and enable late-stage functionalization of drug scaffolds, with a particular focus on diversely strained alkyl environments. We anticipate that these findings will aid in the continued exploration of BCP bioisosteres in complex, drug-like settings.

## EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES

### General procedure for BCP 3-alkylation

To an oven-dried 40 mL vial equipped with a Teflon stir bar and desiccated NaOAc (82 mg, 1.0 mmol, 2.0 equiv.), was added 4CzIPN ([PC-1], 3.94 mg, 5.0 μmol, 0.01 equiv.), copper(II)dibromide (CuBr2, 22.3 mg, 0.1 mmol, 0.2 equiv.), and, if a solid, the limiting alkyl bromide (0.5 mmol, 1.0 equiv.). The vessel was closed and sealed with electrical tape, then back filled under N2 gas. This was followed by addition of anhydrous, degassed acetone (10 mL, 0.05M). If a liquid, the alkyl bromide was introduced via syringe at this step, and the vessel placed under nitrogen gas. The resultant reaction mixture was subsequently stirred within the Integrated Photoreactor (450 nm irradiation) for 0.5 hours. After 0.5 hours, the reaction mixture was opened to air and directly subjected to purification via flash chromatography to afford the desired 3-alkylated product.

### General procedure for BCP 3-(hetero)arylation

To an oven-dried 40 mL vial equipped with a Teflon stir bar and desiccated NaOAc (82 mg, 1.0 mmol, 2.0 equiv.), was added [Ir(dtbbpy)(ppy)2]PF6 ([PC-1], 4.6 mg, 5.0 μmol, 0.01 equiv.), copper bis(2,2,6,6-tetramethyl-3,5-heptanedionate) (Cu(TMHD)2, 107.5 mg, 0.25 mmol, 0.5 equiv.), and, if a solid, the limiting aryl bromide (0.5 mmol, 1.0 equiv.). The vessel was closed and sealed with electrical tape, then back filled under N2 gas. This was followed by addition of anhydrous, degassed acetone (10 mL, 0.05M). If a liquid, the aryl bromide was introduced via syringe at this step, and the vessel placed under nitrogen gas. The resultant reaction mixture was subsequently stirred within the Integrated Photoreactor (450 nm irradiation) for 1 hour. After 1 hour, the reaction mixture was opened to air and directly subjected to purification via flash chromatography to afford the desired 3-arylated product.

### Resource availability:

#### Discussion regarding selection of silane reagent

The tert-butyl-methyl aminosilane reagent was implemented to prevent deactivation of the NHPI redox active ester. It is postulated that the silane reagent generates an equivalent ratio of alkyl amine following the proposed aza-Brook rearrangement and consequently participates in undesired nucleophilic attack of the BCP NHPI reagent. The tert-butyl substituent provides sufficient steric hindrance to disfavor addition into the electrophilic carbon of the NHPI redox active ester. The tert-butyl-methyl aminosilane can be prepared on gram scale, via one-step protocol from commercially available starting materials. Key reagents include triflic acid, supersilane, and tert-butyl-methyl amine (1g, $36 USD at time of writing). Nota bene, supersilane gives drastically lower yield than the optimal tert-butyl-methyl aminosilane reagent. For further reaction optimization data and reaction details See SI Section 4-7, Figures S1–31.

Other experimental details and examples, as well as characterization data, can be found in the Supplemental Information.
